body.heading: Thanksgiving for the harvest, everywhere
paragraphs: When the crops come in, people feast — it may be the oldest party idea there is. Harvest festivals pair gratitude with relief: the work is done, the store cupboards are full, and winter can be faced. The foods differ by continent, but the table is always the centre of it.

In Britain, harvest festivals fill churches and schools with produce that is later shared with those who need it. Germany's Erntedankfest gives thanks with parades and decorated harvest crowns. Korea's Chuseok and China's Mid-Autumn Festival join harvest thanks to family reunion and honouring ancestors, with special foods — songpyeon rice cakes, mooncakes — made and shared.

body.heading: Gratitude with dirt under its nails
paragraphs: Harvest thanks is specific in a way modern gratitude often is not: this wheat, these hands, that rain. Even for families far from farming, the festival suggests a practice — name the year's provisions concretely. The job that paid, the neighbour who helped, the garden that gave three courgettes and a lesson.
Sharing is built into the design. Harvest food was traditionally given away because abundance that is not shared spoils; many festivals still collect for food banks and community kitchens.

body.heading: A harvest table of your own
paragraphs: Any autumn meal can borrow the shape: seasonal food, one round of specific thanks before eating, and something set aside to give away. Children who help choose the donation learn the festival's oldest lesson with their hands.
Let the children decorate the table with what the season offers — leaves, conkers, the last garden flowers. A harvest table should look gathered, not purchased.

description: From harvest crowns to mooncakes, harvest festivals everywhere pair specific gratitude with sharing — a shape any family table can borrow.
